items.title: Foreword
items.text: FOREWORD This document is a synthetic example prepared to exercise the Clause Lab indexer. Its numbering, headings, notes and requirement statements imitate the usual conventions of technical standards, while all wording is invented and carries no normative value. Attention is drawn to the possibility that some of the elements of this example may resemble real documents only in their structure. No rights are claimed on that structure.

items.title: Introduction
items.text:
INTRODUCTION Widgets are small configurable assemblies used in many products. A disciplined life cycle reduces the probability that a widget fault leads to an unsafe condition of the product that embeds it. This example defines a minimum set of processes, activities and records. The requirements are deliberately short so that the regions produced by the indexer can be verified at a glance.
EXAMPLE WIDGETS – LIFE CYCLE PROCESSES

items.title: Scope
items.text: 1 Scope This document specifies life cycle requirements for the development and maintenance of widgets. It applies to widgets delivered alone and to widgets integrated into a larger product.

items.title: Normative references
items.text: 2 Normative references There are no normative references in this document.

items.title: Terms and definitions
items.text: 3 Terms and definitions For the purposes of this document, the following terms and definitions apply.

items.title: widget
items.text: 3.1 widget configurable assembly of parts that performs one function within a product Note 1 to entry: A widget can contain software.

items.title: activity
items.text: 3.2 activity set of one or more interrelated tasks

items.title: record
items.text: 3.3 record document stating results achieved or providing evidence of activities performed

items.title: fault
items.text: 3.4 fault abnormal condition that can cause a widget to fail to perform its function Note 1 to entry: A fault can be latent until a specific input occurs.

items.title: release
items.text: 3.5 release particular version of a widget made available for a specific purpose

items.title: widget class
items.text: 3.6 widget class grouping of widgets according to the severity of the consequences of their faults

items.title: Modification
items.text:
5.2 Modification Modifications to a released widget follow the same process as the original development, scaled to the size of the change. This subclause is intentionally long so that it continues on the following page and the indexer has to draw a region that crosses a page boundary. The maker shall analyse each requested modification before implementing it. The analysis shall identify the parts of the widget affected, the records to be updated and whether the widget class remains valid. When a modification is approved, the maker shall implement it, verify it and update the affected records. Verification shall include a repetition of the tests that could be influenced by the modification.
NOTE 1 A repetition of all tests is acceptable when the influence of the modification cannot be bounded. The maker shall inform the users of the widget about each new release and about known faults that remain in it. [Class B]
NOTE 2 Information can be provided in release notes, labels or electronic notices. Additional guidance for modifications is given in A.2. The following paragraphs describe a typical sequence of events that leads from a field observation to a new release; they are informative. A field observation is reported by a user. The maker evaluates whether the observation reveals a fault. If it does, a modification request is opened and analysed as described above. The modification is then implemented, verified and released together with updated records and user information. Field observation Analysis Implementation Release Figure 1 – Typical modification sequence The maker shall keep the records of each modification together with the records of the release that contains it. [Class A, B]

items.title: General
items.text: A.1 General This annex explains the reasons behind selected requirements. It does not add requirements.

items.title: Modifications
items.text: A.2 Modifications Most faults found after release originate from modifications. Repeating the influenced tests (see 5.2) is the most effective single measure; Table A.1 summarises the effort usually spent. Table A.1 – Typical verification effort Size of modification Share of tests repeated Configuration only about 10 % Local code change about 30 % Interface change up to 100 %

items.title: Classification
items.text: A.3 Classification Two classes are enough for most widgets. A finer classification rarely changes the activities performed and makes the assignment harder to justify.
